title: The Exclusion Principle and the Number 137: Pauli between the Laboratory and the Dream
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Vienna, the christening cup of Ernst Mach
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth 25 April 1900, christening 31 May 1900
stops.campa: Wolfgang Ernst Pauli is born in Vienna on the twenty-fifth of April, first child of the chemist Wolfgang Joseph Pauli and Bertha Camilla Schutz. At the christening five weeks later the physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach stands as godfather and gives the infant a silver cup. The middle name is Mach's own. The man who spent his working life dismantling Newton's absolute space and time gives the boy, before he can speak, his own name and a quarrel with received certainty. A sister, Hertha, follows in 1906.
suggested_refs: The silver christening cup given by Ernst Mach, 31 May 1900

stops.name: Doblinger-Gymnasium, the schoolboy's relativity paper
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He graduates with distinction from the Doblinger-Gymnasium in the nineteenth district, having spent his last school years reading general relativity under the desk. Within two months of the final examination he publishes his first scientific paper, on Einstein's theory of gravitation, in a professional journal. Vienna produces a boy who has outrun the syllabus before anyone thinks to test him against it. He leaves for Munich with the paper already in print and the war ending around him.
suggested_refs: Pauli's first published paper on general relativity, 1918

stops.name: Munich, entering Sommerfeld's seminar
stops.date_confidence: year attested; autumn term inferred
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Ludwig Maximilian University under Arnold Sommerfeld, who reads the eighteen-year-old's relativity paper and thereafter treats him as a colleague. Sommerfeld's seminar is the best school of theoretical physics in Europe and the new student is set to the hardest work in it: the relativity article for the Encyclopedia of Mathematical Sciences, a commission that would normally go to a professor with a chair. He begins it as an undergraduate and works at it for the better part of three years.
suggested_refs: Sommerfeld's theoretical physics seminar at Munich, 1918-1921

stops.name: Munich, Heisenberg across the table
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1920, Heisenberg's entry into the seminar; day defaulted
stops.campa: Werner Heisenberg arrives in Sommerfeld's seminar a year behind him and finds Pauli already installed as the room's merciless intelligence. The two argue physics through Munich nights and settle into a friendship conducted almost entirely as criticism. Heisenberg will send Pauli every paper he writes before he publishes it, and Pauli will tell him without softening what is wrong with it. Neither man ever finds a better reader. The arrangement outlasts a world war and both their marriages.
suggested_refs: The Pauli-Heisenberg correspondence, begun at Munich and running to 1958

stops.name: Munich, the doctorate and the encyclopedia article
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He takes his doctorate under Sommerfeld with a thesis on the quantum theory of ionized diatomic hydrogen, and in the same year finishes the encyclopedia commission: two hundred and thirty-seven pages on relativity, written at twenty-one. Albert Einstein reads it and calls it masterly, remarking that nobody studying the work would guess the age of its author. It is issued separately as a monograph and stands for decades as the standard exposition. He leaves Munich for an assistantship at Gottingen.
suggested_refs: Pauli, Relativitatstheorie (1921), the encyclopedia monograph praised by Einstein

stops.name: Gottingen, assistant to Max Born
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor gives October 1921 through 1922; one summary lens dates the post to 1922, contradiction unresolved
stops.campa: He goes to Gottingen as assistant to Max Born, into the circle where quantum theory is being rewritten sentence by sentence. Born finds him formidable and unpunctual, a young man who works until dawn, misses morning lectures, and corrects senior physicists in seminar without lowering his voice. The appointment lasts barely a year and it places him inside the innermost ring of the coming revolution. He leaves knowing that the anomalous spectra of atoms are the problem nobody can solve.
suggested_refs: Born's Gottingen institute, 1921-1922, and its assistants

stops.name: Copenhagen, the year at Blegdamsvej
stops.date_confidence: academic year 1922-23 attested; month defaulted to the start of term
stops.campa: He spends an academic year at Niels Bohr's institute on Blegdamsvej, where the standing rule is that atomic theory must answer to physical intuition and not to formalism alone. Bohr argues with him as an equal despite the fifteen years between them, and the correspondence begun here runs until Pauli's death. Copenhagen hands him the anomalous Zeeman effect, the splitting of spectral lines no existing theory can account for. It takes him three years, and it costs him the look of a happy man.
stops.quote: How can one look happy when he is thinking about the anomalous Zeeman effect?
stops.quote_source: Cited in Wolfgang Pauli, Writings on Physics and Philosophy, eds. Enz and von Meyenn (1994), p. 15
suggested_refs: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics, Blegdamsvej 17, Copenhagen

stops.name: Hamburg, the lectureship
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He takes a lectureship in theoretical physics at Hamburg and stays five years, the most productive stretch of his life. Students find him alarming: he sits through half a seminar in silence, muttering and rocking, then erupts to correct the speaker in front of the room. Colleagues learn that a manuscript sent to him comes back flayed. In these years he acquires the title his own generation uses for him without irony, the conscience of physics, and the habit of judgment he never afterward puts down.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg physics institute under Wilhelm Lenz and Otto Stern, 1923-1928

stops.name: Hamburg, the exclusion principle
stops.date_confidence: the two-valued degree of freedom is proposed late in 1924; the exclusion paper is received in January 1925
stops.campa: Chasing the anomalous Zeeman effect he posits at the end of 1924 a fourth quantum number, a two-valued degree of freedom belonging to the electron alone, and then the rule that follows from it: no two electrons in an atom may share the same set of quantum numbers. The periodic table falls out of it whole. Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit name the two-valuedness spin, and in 1927 Pauli writes the matrices that describe it. Satyendra Nath Bose, reading Pauli's work in Dacca, has already reached the other statistics.
suggested_refs: Pauli, 'Uber den Zusammenhang des Abschlusses der Elektronengruppen im Atom mit der Komplexstruktur der Spektren', Zeitschrift fur Physik 31 (1925), 765-783

stops.name: Hamburg, Otto Stern's laboratory
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources consulted; placed within the Hamburg years 1923-1928
stops.campa: In Otto Stern's laboratory a superstition takes hold among men who believe in nothing but measurement: apparatus fails when Pauli is in the building. Glassware cracks, vacuum seals give, alignments drift, and Pauli touches nothing. Stern, who is his friend, comes to insist that he keep out of the experimental hall during delicate runs and holds their conversations at the door. Physicists give the pattern a name, the Pauli effect, and go on collecting instances of it for the next thirty years.
stops.quote: Pauli was such a good theoretical physicist that something usually broke in the lab whenever he merely stepped across the threshold.
stops.quote_source: George Gamow, Thirty Years That Shook Physics (1966), p. 64
suggested_refs: Otto Stern's molecular beam laboratory at Hamburg
sources: George Gamow, Thirty Years That Shook Physics (1966)

segments.name: Solvay, Vienna, and the Zurich Chair

stops.name: Brussels, the fifth Solvay and the line about Dirac
stops.date_confidence: attested; the congress sits 24-29 October 1927
stops.campa: At the fifth Solvay Congress in the Parc Leopold the whole of quantum physics sits at one table: Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrodinger, Dirac, Born. The argument over whether the new mechanics is a complete account runs through the sessions and out into the dinners. Paul Dirac, pressed at table on religion, delivers a flat denial of any use for God in physics, and Pauli, who has listened without speaking, supplies the summary the room remembers. He is twenty-seven and holds his place among them by right.
stops.quote: There is no God and Dirac is his Prophet.
stops.quote_source: Remark at the Fifth Solvay Conference, October 1927, recorded in Werner Heisenberg, Der Teil und das Ganze (1969), p. 119
suggested_refs: The 1927 Solvay group photograph on the steps of the Institut International de Physique
sources: Heisenberg, Der Teil und das Ganze (1969)

stops.name: Vienna, his mother's death
stops.date_confidence: 1927 attested by MacTutor and German Wikipedia; the day is not established and is defaulted; English Wikipedia's placement of the death at the end of 1930 is a contradiction left standing
stops.campa: Bertha Camilla Pauli, journalist and pacifist, dies in Vienna by poison after her husband's affair becomes public. Her son is twenty-seven and does not speak of it easily afterward; his father remarries within the year, to a woman younger than Wolfgang, and the estrangement between father and son dates from there. Later accounts drag this death forward three years and fuse it with his divorce into a single collapse. It belongs here, in a year that otherwise looks from outside like a triumph.
suggested_refs: Bertha Camilla Pauli (1878-1927), journalist, in the Wiener Personlichkeiten registers

stops.name: Zurich, the chair at the ETH
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He is appointed professor of theoretical physics at the Eidgenossische Technische Hochschule, the chair he holds, with one long wartime interruption, until he dies. Zurich becomes the fixed point of his geography: he will leave it for Princeton, for Stockholm, for the lecture terraces above Ascona, and return each time to this address. He is twenty-eight. The city that will watch two marriages, a breakdown, an analysis, and a death begins its involvement with him now.
suggested_refs: The ETH chair of theoretical physics, held by Pauli 1928-1958

stops.name: Zurich, Oppenheimer under the lash
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929 in the Oppenheimer material; month follows that record
stops.campa: Paul Ehrenfest sends the young Robert Oppenheimer to Zurich with the explicit instruction that Pauli grind the flashiness out of him. Oppenheimer arrives brilliant and unfinished and meets a teacher who declines to be impressed, who interrupts, who withholds praise as a matter of method. He calls the months the making of him and speaks of Pauli for the rest of his life as the man whose judgment he most wanted. Zurich sharpens him the way a stone sharpens a blade, by removing material.
suggested_refs: Oppenheimer's Zurich year under Pauli, 1929

stops.name: Berlin, marriage to Kathe Deppner
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor gives Berlin, 23 December 1929, against one summary that places the wedding in Zurich
stops.campa: He marries Kathe Margarethe Deppner in Berlin four days before Christmas. She is a cabaret dancer, in love with a chemist, and does not trouble to conceal it. Colleagues who know Pauli only as an instrument of judgment cannot place the match at all. The marriage lasts under a year. He is twenty-nine, at the height of his powers in physics and without any working knowledge of how to live, and the collapse of this house opens the worst two years of his life.
suggested_refs: The Berlin marriage register entry of 23 December 1929

stops.name: Vienna, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor gives Vienna, 29 November 1930, against one summary that places the decree in Zurich
stops.campa: The divorce from Kathe Deppner is granted in Vienna on the twenty-ninth of November, less than a year after the wedding. He is drinking heavily and in public, quarreling in bars, and lecturing at the ETH the next morning in the same unbroken voice. Vienna, which gave him a christening cup and then a dead mother, now gives him this. Five days after the decree he sits down in Zurich and writes the open letter that invents a particle nobody can detect.
suggested_refs: The Vienna divorce decree of 29 November 1930

stops.name: Zurich, the letter to the radioactive ladies and gentlemen
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated 4 December 1930
stops.campa: Unable to leave Zurich for the radioactivity meeting at Tubingen because of a ball he will not miss, he writes to the assembled physicists instead: Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen. The energy missing from beta decay, he proposes, is carried off by a neutral particle of very small mass that escapes every instrument they have. He calls the idea a desperate remedy and doubts it can ever be confirmed. Enrico Fermi will build the theory of the weak interaction on it and give the thing its name, neutrino.
stops.quote: I have done a terrible thing. I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected.
stops.quote_source: Statement of 1930, reported by Frederick Reines, foreword to Christine Sutton, Spaceship Neutrino (1992), p. xi
suggested_refs: The open letter of 4 December 1930 to the Tubingen radioactivity congress

segments.name: The Crisis and the Dream Diary

stops.name: Ann Arbor, the summer symposium
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the Michigan symposium runs in summer, month inferred
stops.campa: He crosses to Michigan for the summer symposium in theoretical physics, part of the traffic of European theorists into American departments in the years when the crossing is still a choice. American students meet the interrupting lecturer whose reputation reached them long before he did. He is drinking, and the men around him notice. He returns to Zurich with the disorder in his private life untouched by the ocean and with six months left before he knocks at a psychiatrist's door.
suggested_refs: The University of Michigan summer symposium in theoretical physics, Ann Arbor

stops.name: Zurich, the letter to Peierls on semiconductors
stops.date_confidence: attested; letter dated 29 September 1931
stops.campa: He writes to Rudolf Peierls, who has been asking him about conduction in solids, a verdict of the kind he issues without hedging: the subject is a filthy mess and may not correspond to anything real. It is one of the worst calls he ever makes and he makes it in exactly the register he uses when he is right. His authority is such that the letter is remembered by the men who ignored it, and repeated for the rest of the century by everyone who builds transistors.
stops.quote: One shouldn't work on semiconductors, that is a filthy mess; who knows whether any semiconductors exist.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Rudolf Peierls, 29 September 1931, in Wolfgang Pauli, Wissenschaftlicher Briefwechsel, Band II (1985), p. 94
suggested_refs: Pauli's Wissenschaftlicher Briefwechsel, Band II, the Peierls correspondence
sources: Wolfgang Pauli, Wissenschaftlicher Briefwechsel, Band II (1985)

stops.name: Kusnacht, at Jung's door
stops.date_confidence: January 1932 attested; day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: On his father's advice he goes out along the lake to the house Carl Gustav Jung built at Kusnacht, a short train ride from the ETH, and asks for help. He is thirty-one, divorced, drinking, and unable to give an account of his own condition in the only language he trusts. Jung sees at once that the case is unusual: a patient whose analytic intelligence can dismantle any interpretation offered to him. He declines to take Pauli on directly. He hands him to an assistant and asks him for his dreams.
suggested_refs: Jung's house and consulting rooms at Seestrasse 228, Kusnacht

stops.name: Kusnacht, Erna Rosenbaum and the dream diary
stops.date_confidence: the treatment with Rosenbaum is attested for 1932 to 1934; the month of its start is inferred
stops.campa: The analysis proper is conducted by Erna Rosenbaum, a young physician in Jung's circle, and runs to 1934. Pauli does with this what he does with any problem: he keeps a record. He writes down his dreams, hundreds of them, mandalas and clocks and a figure he calls the dark man, and the geometry in them keeps rhyming with the mathematics of his day work. Jung reads the series as documents rather than as sessions and prints more than four hundred of them without a name, as the dreams of a scientific man.
suggested_refs: C.G. Jung, Psychology and Alchemy (1944), the anonymous dream series

stops.name: Zurich, marriage to Franca Bertram
stops.date_confidence: 1934 attested; the exact day is given as 4 April in one lens and not independently confirmed
stops.campa: He marries Franziska Bertram, called Franca, and the household holds for the remaining twenty-four years of his life. She manages the practical world around a man who has no aptitude for it, keeps his hours, receives his colleagues, and reads him accurately. Those who watched the unraveling of 1930 mark this year as the one in which he visibly rights himself. Her own account of him, given long afterward, is not sentimental and does not pretend the analysis finished the work.
stops.quote: He tried to live without admitting reality. And his unworldliness stemmed precisely from his belief that that was possible.
stops.quote_source: Franca Pauli, quoted in Arthur I. Miller, 137: Jung, Pauli, and the Pursuit of a Scientific Obsession (2009); the same passage appears in Abraham Pais, The Genius of Science
suggested_refs: Franca Pauli's recollections as recorded by Miller and Pais
sources: Abraham Pais, The Genius of Science

stops.name: The honeymoon road, the car that will not start
stops.date_confidence: undated within 1934; the place of the breakdown is not recorded and the coordinates mark Zurich as departure point only
stops.campa: On the honeymoon journey with Franca the car stops and cannot be made to go again, with nothing wrong that any mechanic can find. Pauli reports the failure afterward as evidence, and means it: the effect that carries his name has followed him out of the laboratories and into his own marriage. He treats the pattern as half a joke among physicists and half an open question, a man who has spent fifteen years demanding rigor and cannot get this one thing to behave.
suggested_refs: The honeymoon breakdown of 1934, in the Pauli effect literature

stops.name: Princeton, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He takes a visiting professorship at the Institute for Advanced Study, where Einstein has been settled two years since leaving Germany for good. The two have argued about the same physics from opposite ends of it for fifteen years and find in New Jersey a wary regard for one another. Pauli's American connections are still occasional in 1935, a matter of invitations accepted and returned. Within five years they will be the only door out of a continent closing behind him.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, in the years of the European emigration

stops.name: Zurich, made German without asking
stops.date_confidence: the Anschluss is attested to 12 March 1938; the day of Pauli's reclassification is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: Germany annexes Austria in March and Pauli, holding an Austrian passport, is reclassified overnight as a German citizen. He is of Jewish descent on his father's side, a professor in a neutral country, and now the subject of a state that would arrest him at its own border. He applies for Swiss citizenship and is refused. The chair at the ETH is secure; the legal ground under the man holding it is not, and from this year he begins to look across the Atlantic in earnest.
suggested_refs: The 1938 Anschluss and the automatic German citizenship of Austrian nationals abroad

stops.name: Princeton, the war years
stops.date_confidence: 1940 attested for the emigration and for the spin-statistics paper; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses to Princeton for the duration, a German-classified national who cannot travel Europe safely, and takes a professorship of theoretical physics at the Institute. Here he re-derives the spin-statistics theorem, proving that a particle's spin decides which statistics it obeys, the deepest justification his exclusion principle ever receives. Physicists he trained go to Los Alamos; he does not. He works on meson theory and keeps up by letter the correspondence with Jung that Kusnacht began.
suggested_refs: Pauli's 1940 spin-statistics paper, written at the Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: Princeton, the prize handed over at a reception
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Princeton celebration is held on 10 December 1945
stops.campa: The 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics is announced for the exclusion principle, on a nomination written by Albert Einstein, and postwar travel makes Stockholm unreachable that December. Princeton holds a reception for him on the tenth instead, at which Einstein rises and speaks of Pauli as his own successor. He is forty-five and has waited twenty years for a discovery made by a young lecturer in Hamburg to be named. What Stockholm owes him is delivered in a hall in New Jersey.
suggested_refs: The Princeton Nobel reception of 10 December 1945 and Einstein's remarks

segments.name: Zurich Again: Physics and the Psyche

stops.name: Zurich, the return and the American passport
stops.date_confidence: 1946 attested for both the naturalization and the return to the ETH; the months are not established and are inferred
stops.campa: He becomes a naturalized citizen of the United States and then, in the same year, sails back to the ETH chair he left six years earlier. The Zurich he returns to is a city the war never touched, in a country that refused him papers at the moment he needed them. He resumes the professorship and the lecturing, and the conversations out at Kusnacht start again as something other than treatment: two men working the same problem from the physics and from the dreams, in writing, at length.
suggested_refs: Pauli's US naturalization certificate, 1946

stops.name: Stockholm, the lecture a year late
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Nobel lecture is recorded as delivered in December 1946, the exact day taken from the Nobel records and not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: A year after the prize is announced he travels to Stockholm and gives the Nobel lecture in person, closing the ceremony the war interrupted. He traces the argument from Niels Bohr's atomic model through the anomalous Zeeman effect to the four quantum numbers and the rule that no two electrons may share them, and gives the credit to the problem rather than to the man who solved it. It is the fullest public account he ever offers of how the exclusion principle was found.
suggested_refs: Pauli's Nobel lecture, 'Exclusion Principle and Quantum Mechanics', Stockholm, December 1946

stops.name: Zurich, the vase at the founding of the Jung Institute
stops.date_confidence: 1948 attested for the founding of the institute; the April dating given in one lens is unsourced and the month is defaulted; the founding premises are not located, so the pin is the city
stops.campa: At the founding festivities of the C.G. Jung Institute a china flower vase falls to the floor and breaks as Pauli comes into the building, with nothing near it. The room takes it at once for the effect that bears his name, and Pauli, delighted rather than embarrassed, takes it for material. He is writing that year a private manuscript for Jung on the way physical concepts surface in dream images. An institute founded on meaningful coincidence opens with an object breaking beside him.
suggested_refs: Pauli, 'Moderne Beispiele zur Hintergrundsphysik' (1948), the manuscript sent to Jung
sources: Wikipedia, 'C. G. Jung Institute in Zurich'

stops.name: Ascona, Eranos above the lake
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Eranos lecture on Kepler is placed in the Ascona meetings of the late 1940s; the exact year and month are not confirmed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He lectures at the Eranos gathering on the hill above Lake Maggiore, before a company of orientalists, mythographers and analysts who have never had a Nobel physicist among them. His subject is Johannes Kepler: how an inherited image of the trinity, held before there was any evidence for it, shaped the astronomy Kepler believed he was reading straight off the sky. It is an argument about where scientific ideas come from, and it is also, without saying so, an argument about himself.
suggested_refs: The Eranos meetings at Monte Verita, Ascona, and Pauli's Kepler essay

stops.name: Zurich, the letter to Fierz on reality
stops.date_confidence: attested; letter dated 12 August 1948
stops.campa: He writes to Markus Fierz, his former assistant and the man he uses as a sounding board for everything he cannot say to physicists, that the word reality is itself the problem. The layman uses it for whatever is self-evident to him. Pauli holds that building a new idea of reality, one that can carry both the observed world and the observer who observes it, is the hardest task of the age. He is working at it in two languages and does not consider them separate languages.
stops.quote: The layman always means, when he says 'reality' that he is speaking of something self-evidently known; whereas to me it seems the most important and exceedingly difficult task of our time is to work on the construction of a new idea of reality.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Markus Fierz, 12 August 1948, cited in Suzanne Gieser, The Innermost Kernel (2005)
suggested_refs: The Pauli-Fierz correspondence of the late 1940s
sources: Suzanne Gieser, The Innermost Kernel: Depth Psychology and Quantum Physics (2005)

stops.name: Zurich, the Swiss papers at last
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: Eleven years after the Anschluss made him German and the Confederation turned down his application, Switzerland grants Pauli citizenship. It is the third nationality of his adult life and the one that holds. The city where he has taught for twenty years, where his analysis was conducted across the lake and where he will die, becomes his legal home as well as his address. He keeps the American passport alongside it. He is forty-eight, and he does not move again.
suggested_refs: Pauli's Swiss naturalization, 1949

stops.name: Gottingen station, the train he never leaves
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources consulted; one lens places the incident in 1950 and another in the 1930s, and the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: An expensive measuring apparatus in the physics institute at Gottingen fails without explanation, and James Franck writes to Pauli in Zurich to report it as a joke, the one instance of the effect for which he plainly cannot be blamed. Pauli writes back that at the hour in question he was changing trains at Gottingen station on a journey from Zurich, without once setting foot off the platform. Physicists repeat the story for decades as the cleanest case anyone recorded.
suggested_refs: The Gottingen station anecdote in the Pauli effect literature

stops.name: Princeton, the cyclotron burns
stops.date_confidence: February 1950 attested; the day is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: On a visit to Princeton University the cyclotron in the Palmer Physical Laboratory catches fire and burns while Pauli is in the building. He asks aloud, half seriously, whether the mischief belongs to the effect named after him. The instances now run from Hamburg to Gottingen to New Jersey and colleagues no longer bother suppressing their laughter when equipment fails near him. He never settles, in public or in his letters, whether the pattern amuses him or indicts everything he teaches.
suggested_refs: The Palmer Physical Laboratory cyclotron fire, Princeton University, February 1950

stops.name: Zurich, Naturerklarung und Psyche
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: Rascher Verlag publishes the one book Pauli and Carl Gustav Jung make together: Jung's essay on synchronicity as an acausal connecting principle, bound with Pauli's study of the archetypal ideas standing behind Kepler's astronomy. Twenty years after he came out to Kusnacht as a patient, the physicist appears as a co-author. Physicists read it with embarrassment for a colleague they consider unassailable elsewhere, and go on citing his exclusion principle. He does not defend the book.
suggested_refs: Naturerklarung und Psyche (Rascher, Zurich, 1952)

stops.name: Zurich, God is not a weak left-hander
stops.date_confidence: the Wu experiment runs in December 1956 and its results are announced in January 1957; the day of Pauli's remark is not established
stops.campa: Word arrives from Columbia that parity is not conserved in the weak interaction: nature tells left from right, and the mirror symmetry Pauli had treated as beyond argument is broken. He had bet Victor Weisskopf a large sum that the experiments would find nothing. He pays, and puts his objection into the only form that carries the size of it, which is theological. The result stands. The last of his certainties about symmetry goes down twenty-three months before he does.
stops.quote: I cannot believe that God is a weak left-hander.
stops.quote_source: Pauli on the confirmation of parity violation, 1957, quoted in Leon M. Lederman and Christopher T. Hill, Beyond the God Particle (2013)
suggested_refs: The Wu experiment on parity violation, Columbia University, 1956-1957
sources: Lederman and Hill, Beyond the God Particle (2013)

stops.name: Munich, the world formula with Heisenberg
stops.date_confidence: 1958 attested for the collaboration and its collapse; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: Werner Heisenberg pursues a single field equation for all of matter and draws Pauli in as collaborator at the Max Planck Institute, newly moved to Munich, and for a few months the two men who met in Sommerfeld's seminar thirty-eight years earlier work on one formula together. Pauli's enthusiasm curdles into open scorn within weeks. He withdraws his name and mocks the announcement in public. It is the last thing they do together and it ends the way their arguments always ended.
suggested_refs: The Heisenberg-Pauli unified field equation of 1958 and its public collapse

stops.name: Zurich, the blank canvas sent to Gamow
stops.date_confidence: 1958 attested; the month is not established and is inferred from its place in the world formula quarrel
stops.campa: He posts George Gamow a sheet of paper carrying an empty rectangle and one line of caption beneath it. The joke is aimed at Heisenberg's world formula and at every theory announced before it works, and it is the most economical review Pauli ever writes. The two have kept up an exchange of this kind for years. He is fifty-eight, in his last year, and still the man to whom the discipline sends its unfinished work for a verdict it is not going to enjoy.
stops.quote: This is to show the world that I can paint like Titian. Only technical details are missing.
stops.quote_source: Caption beneath a blank rectangle sent to George Gamow, 1958, cited in Michio Kaku, Hyperspace (1994), p. 137
suggested_refs: Pauli's blank-canvas letter to George Gamow, 1958

stops.name: Berkeley, misunderstanding at a deeper level
stops.date_confidence: May 1958 attested by the citing source; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: In California in the spring he tells the young historian of physics Jagdish Mehra what the trade can realistically expect of itself: that the best most of them can hope for is to misunderstand at a deeper level. He is speaking as a man who spent thirty years failing to derive why the fine structure constant sits so near one part in a hundred and thirty-seven, and who never once suggested the failure was somebody else's. It is the last account he gives of his own work.
stops.quote: The best that most of us can hope to achieve in physics is simply to misunderstand at a deeper level.
stops.quote_source: Remark to Jagdish Mehra, Berkeley, California, May 1958, cited in Mehra and Rechenberg, The Historical Development of Quantum Theory (2000)
suggested_refs: Mehra and Rechenberg, The Historical Development of Quantum Theory, on Pauli's last year
sources: Mehra and Rechenberg, The Historical Development of Quantum Theory (2000)

stops.name: Zurich, room 137 at the Rotkreuzspital
stops.date_confidence: attested; death on 15 December 1958 of pancreatic cancer, in room 137
stops.campa: Pancreatic cancer brings him to the Rotkreuzspital on the Gloriastrasse. His assistant Charles Enz comes to visit, and Pauli asks him whether he has seen the number on the door. It is 137, the integer nearest the inverse of the fine structure constant, the number he had wanted his whole working life to derive from first principles and never could. He dies in that room on the fifteenth of December, aged fifty-eight, with the constant still unexplained and the coincidence holding the last word.
stops.quote: Did you see the room number?
stops.quote_source: Reported remark to Charles Enz at the Rotkreuzspital, December 1958, cited in Charles P. Enz, No Time to Be Brief (2002)
suggested_refs: The former Rotkreuzspital on the Gloriastrasse, Zurich, now the Careum Campus
sources: Charles P. Enz, No Time to Be Brief (2002)

stops.name: Zollikon, the grave above the lake
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Friedhof Zollikon is attested by the gravestone; the date of the funeral is not established, and the date given here is the date of death
stops.campa: He is buried in the cemetery at Zollikon on the slope above the lake, a few kilometers from the ETH where he taught and from the house at Kusnacht where Carl Gustav Jung read four hundred of his dreams as a document. Nothing of the unified account he wanted is finished on his desk: not the fine structure constant, not the world formula, not the physics of the psyche the two of them were still writing toward. The stone stands there with his name and the two dates.
suggested_refs: Pauli's gravestone at the Friedhof Zollikon Dorf

stops.name: Vienna, a street in Weidlingau
stops.date_confidence: 1969 attested for the designation; month and day not established, defaulted
stops.campa: The city of his birth names a street for him in Weidlingau, at the far western edge of the Penzing district, in 1969. It is a small residential lane and it carries his full name. Vienna christened him with Ernst Mach standing over the font, schooled him at Dobling, buried his mother, and granted his divorce, and he left at eighteen and lived his adult life elsewhere. Sixty-nine years after the christening cup the city puts him back on its own map, in an outer suburb, spelled out.
suggested_refs: Wolfgang-Pauli-Gasse, Weidlingau, Penzing, Vienna, designated 1969

stops.name: Honggerberg, the street, the bust, and the crater
stops.date_confidence: no single date; the sources consulted give no naming year for the Honggerberg street, the bust or the annual lectures, so this year is a placeholder rather than an attestation. The lunar crater Pauli was designated by the IAU in 1970 and the asteroid (13093) Wolfgangpauli carries no naming date in the source consulted
stops.campa: The largest street on the ETH science campus at Honggerberg is Wolfgang-Pauli-Strasse; the school he served for thirty years holds annual lectures under his name and keeps a bust of him cast by Otto Charles Banninger. A street in Gottingen carries the name, and so does the largest lecture hall of the Hamburg physics institutes. An asteroid carries it. So does a crater a hundred kilometers wide on the far side of the Moon, at forty-five degrees south and one hundred and thirty-seven degrees east.
suggested_refs: Wolfgang-Pauli-Strasse and the Banninger bust at ETH Honggerberg; the lunar crater Pauli at 45.24 S, 137.52 E
